transcript:
[00:00] Sam Carter: Hi everyone, thank you for joining. quick intro — I'm Sam from Redwood, AE. with me is Priya and Liam on the SE side.
[00:08] Dr. Elena Voss: Thanks Sam. We, uh, appreciate you making time. Borealis has a bunch of regulatory constraints so wanted to talk through an air-gapped private deployment, like fully offline.
[00:22] Priya Rao: Absolutely, Elena. We work with several pharma customers on the private, on-prem option. to kick off, can you describe the environment — totally offline? OR is there a bastion host?
[00:34] Mark Chen: It is basically air-gapped. no outbound internet from the compute cluster. we have a management VLAN that can reach an internal patch-server but nothing leaves the DHA — sorry — the DMZ. updates generally come via signed images on encrypted USB, internal courier.
[00:47] Liam Ortiz: okay noted. so for Redwood Private we support air-gapped installs; main items are initial package transfer, image signing, and an offline licensing/activation flow. the activation can be done via a token exchange using an intermediary jump host or via an offline key file.
[01:04] Asha Patel: security is primary. we need FIPS-validated crypto, HSM/KMS integration, audit logs for all model requests, and the ability to retain logs for 7 years. also SOC2 is something your team supports?
[01:16] Sam Carter: yes we have SOC2 and ISO evidence; we'll send the pack. on the HSM front, we integrate with customer HSM over network or can support local key import for air-gapped installs. Priya, can you explain the key import flow briefly?
[01:28] Priya Rao: yeah. for air-gapped we do two supported patterns: 1) bring-your-own-key: customer exports a wrapped key from their HSM and we import into the server's keystore (we provide a tool that validates signatures offline); 2) temporary activation token that the customer pastes into the installer that binds to their org id, token generated from the control plane by an authorized Redwood admin and transferred via secure courier. both patterns have been used.
[01:49] Tom Reyes: for model updates, what does that look like? Our models will be internally trained and can't leave the network.
[01:55] Priya Rao: model artifacts can be packaged as tarballs with signature metadata. we have a checksum and signing verification step in the on-prem manager. also we support loading models from an NFS mount or local disk. if you train internally you can drop the signed package into the /opt/redwood/models and the manager will validate and import.
[02:12] Dr. Elena Voss: patching cadence — we run quarterly maintenance windows and cannot accept unscheduled restarts. how disruptive is an update?
[02:20] Liam Ortiz: most updates are rolling; runtime supports graceful worker drain and health checks. for major runtime upgrades there may be short windowed restarts for all nodes depending on kernel changes — we can coordinate to fit your maintenance windows.
[02:33] Mark Chen: hardware — we're evaluating H100 vs A100-FX. we have limited rack power and cooling in our onsite data center. any guidance?
[02:42] Priya Rao: performance-wise H100s give uplift for many models, but A100 via 80GB has solid perf for our curated open models. NVLink or PCIe topology matters for multi-GPU KV cache and large context workloads. we'll share a recommended matrix: throughput/latency per model vs card type.
[02:58] Asha Patel: compliance — can we get immutable logs and an exportable audit trail? and is there RBAC that integrates with our SAML provider?
[03:06] Sam Carter: yes to both. RBAC integrates with SAML/SSO; audit logs are available and we can ship them to your internal SIEM via a secure collector. for air-gapped setups we provide an offline log export tool that produces signed archives you can ingest.
[03:20] Dr. Elena Voss: latency is important for clinical decision support. what are we looking at for per-request latency on a 2k token response for a medium model?
[03:29] Priya Rao: ballpark, on a single H100 80GB instance, median token latency we see for certain decoder models is X — sorry that's too specific — generally sub-second per token for smaller models but for 2k total response end-to-end you should plan for several hundred milliseconds per token; we'll include benchmark numbers per model. our Optimize recommendations around batching and prefix caching often drop cost without compromising median SLAs.
[03:52] Tom Reyes: offline benchmarking — can Redwood run an internal benchmark pack against our hardware?
[03:58] Liam Ortiz: yes, we do a bench-run as part of the POC. we can run a local runner that you execute and then share the results; if you allow us, we can also bring a small appliance onsite, but given air-gap that might be more complicated.
[04:12] Mark Chen: network constraints: we can't have any egress to public cloud. is that fully supported for telemetry and crash reporting?
[04:20] Priya Rao: telemetry is optional — in air-gapped mode telemetry is off by default. logs and metrics are stored locally, and you can configure a push to your internal monitoring. crash dumps are collected locally and can be exported in signed archives for Redwood support review under a signed NDA.
[04:38] Asha Patel: something about legal — we need an indemnity clause and clear data residency in the contract; policy folks will require that. also about backups — do you support encrypted snapshots and do they ever leave the network?
[04:50] Sam Carter: backups are configurable. for air-gapped customers, snapshots are stored only on customer-managed storage and don't leave the network unless you choose to export; we support encryption-at-rest with customer-managed keys. we'll have legal coordinate on indemnities in the SOW.
[05:05] Dr. Elena Voss: timeline — if we move forward, what's a typical POC timeline?
[05:10] Sam Carter: typical POC is 6–12 weeks: week 0 infra prep & install, weeks 1–2 baseline benchmarks and smoke tests, weeks 3–8 integration and workload tests, final week for handover and runbook. for regulated customers we add extra audits so plan for 12 weeks.
[05:25] Tom Reyes: what about model variance and fallback? if we lose a heavy GPU node, can requests be routed to smaller quantized model?
[05:32] Priya Rao: yes we support model variants and automated fallback. routing policies can be local to the cluster and we can configure an elastic pool or a smaller quantized model chain to keep latency bounded.
[05:45] Dr. Elena Voss: price is a question. Capital spend vs subscription?
[05:49] Sam Carter: for Private On-prem we do a license + support model; there is a platform fee, plus optional add-ons (extended observability retention, premium SLA). for Dedicated vs Private there's tradeoff: Dedicated removes infra ops burden but doesn't meet your air-gap constraints. we'll follow up with a pricing sheet and a 3-month POC number.
[06:05] Mark Chen: one more: patch provenance — how do we verify software releases?
[06:09] Liam Ortiz: all builds are signed; the manager verifies signatures and we keep a release manifest. we can provide reproducible build hashes and signing keys for your audit team.
[06:20] Asha Patel: SSO integration: we use Okta and enforce SCIM groups for role assignment, can Redwood map groups to RBAC roles?
[06:27] Priya Rao: yes, we map SCIM groups to roles, and can run attribute-based access controls. we'll include a sample SCIM config in the pack.
[06:36] Dr. Elena Voss: ok, this is helpful. next steps recap?
[06:39] Sam Carter: action recap — we'll send security artifacts incl SOC2/ISO, hardware recommendations with H100/A100 guidance, on-prem installer docs and offline key import steps, and a proposed SOW for a 3-month POC. schedule infra deep-dive with Mark and Tom next week.
[06:57] Tom Reyes: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[07:00] Sam Carter: thanks, we'll follow up.
[54:00] (call end)
